entry.title: Reproducing Figure 3: How often is each recurrence depth sampled?

link.title: Reproducing Figure 3: How often is each recurrence depth sampled?

entry.content:
What I reimplemented

During training, the authors sample how many times to run the recurrent block. I reproduced Figure 3 by implementing the sampling rule from Section 3.3 and drawing one million recurrence counts with $\bar r = 32$ and $\sigma = 0.5$. Paper, Section 3.3

The code

Each draw starts with a normal random variable tau. Its exponential gives the rate for a Poisson draw. Adding one ensures that the recurrent block runs at least once.

mu = np.log(r_bar) - sigma**2 / 2
tau = rng.normal(loc=mu, scale=sigma, size=n)
rate = np.exp(tau)
r = rng.poisson(lam=rate) + 1

Full code and results (Jupyter notebook)

Results

Statistic Figure 3 Reproduction
Mean 33.0 33.002
Median 29 29
Mode 24 24

All three statistics match Figure 3 at the precision reported in the paper.

What I learned

The most common training depth was 24, even though the average was 33. The histogram shows why: occasional draws with many recurrences pull the mean above both the mode and the median. Seeing all three on the same plot made the training schedule easier to interpret.
entry.summary: Reproducing the distribution of training depths from Section 3.3.

entry.title: Can we make machine think more like humans

link.title: Can we make machine think more like humans

entry.content:
Motivation

When we solve a problem, we don’t always approach it in the same way. Some questions are simple enough that we can answer them almost immediately. Others require us to stop and think for a while.

What’s interesting is that we can often estimate how much effort a question will require before we even start solving it. But that estimate isn’t always right. Sometimes a problem looks easy at first, and only after working on it do we realize that we need to think more deeply.

There is another aspect of human reasoning that I find particularly interesting: when a problem becomes too complicated to solve entirely in our heads, we take out a pen and paper.

Writing down intermediate calculations allows us to break a difficult problem into smaller parts, keep track of what we have already discovered, and use those results later. We don’t necessarily write down every thought. We usually start writing when we feel that doing everything mentally is becoming difficult.

I think there is a natural connection between this behavior and reasoning in language models.

The Huginn paper introduces a recurrent Transformer that can perform additional computation in its hidden states before predicting the next token. This resembles the internal part of human reasoning: thinking without necessarily saying or writing anything.

On the other hand, Chain-of-Thought (CoT) can be viewed as the model’s pen and paper. By generating intermediate reasoning steps, the model creates information that it can refer to when making subsequent predictions.

This raises a question:

Instead of forcing a language model to always think for a fixed amount of time or always generate Chain-of-Thought, can we teach it to decide when each approach is useful?

Proposed Idea: A Reasoning Controller

I propose extending Huginn with a single lightweight controller that dynamically decides how the model should allocate its reasoning computation.

The controller would operate both before and during the reasoning process.

Initially, it would examine the question’s representation, produced by Huginn’s prelude, and estimate how much internal computation is needed. Rather than committing to a fixed budget, it would choose an action and then reevaluate the situation after that action has been completed.

As Huginn continues reasoning, the same controller would examine its updated hidden state and decide what to do next.

The controller would have four possible actions:

  • THINK(4): Perform four additional recurrent iterations without generating text.
  • THINK(8): Perform eight additional recurrent iterations without generating text.
  • WRITE: Generate an intermediate reasoning step, similar to writing something down on paper.
  • ANSWER: Stop reasoning and generate the final answer.

We define the action space as:

\[\mathcal{A}= \{\operatorname{THINK}(4),\operatorname{THINK}(8), \operatorname{WRITE},\operatorname{ANSWER}\}.\]

At the beginning, the controller primarily uses the question’s representation to make an initial decision. After recurrent iterations have been performed, it can also use the information accumulated in Huginn’s hidden state.

For example, the model could choose:

\[\operatorname{THINK}(8) \rightarrow \operatorname{THINK}(4) \rightarrow \operatorname{WRITE} \rightarrow \operatorname{THINK}(8) \rightarrow \operatorname{ANSWER}.\]

For a simpler question, it might choose:

\[\operatorname{THINK}(4)\rightarrow\operatorname{ANSWER}.\]

The important point is that we don’t need separate predictors for estimating the initial difficulty and deciding what to do later. The same controller makes both decisions, using the information available at each stage.

This is also closer to how people approach difficult problems. We initially estimate how much thinking is necessary, but we keep reconsidering that estimate as we work.

Model Architecture

The proposed architecture consists of Huginn and one small reasoning controller.

Given an input sequence $x$, Huginn’s prelude produces:

\[e=P(x).\]

At recurrent iteration $k$, the model maintains a hidden state $s_k$. The recurrent computation can be written as:

\[s_{k+1}=R(A(s_k,e)),\]

where $R$ is the recurrent Transformer core and $A$ is the input adapter.

The controller receives a representation of the prelude output, the current recurrent state, and information about the computation already performed.

Its policy is:

\[\boxed{ \pi_\phi(a\mid e,h_k,k) }\]

where:

  • $e$ represents the question’s prelude output.
  • $h_k$ is a summary of the current recurrent hidden state.
  • $k$ is the number of recurrent iterations already performed.
  • $a\in\mathcal A$ is the selected action.
  • $\phi$ denotes the controller’s trainable parameters.

The controller could be implemented as a small feedforward neural network (FFN), followed by a softmax over the four actions.

When it chooses THINK(4) or THINK(8), Huginn performs the requested number of recurrent iterations, and the updated hidden state is passed back to the same controller.

When it chooses WRITE, Huginn enters a special generation mode, indicated by a token such as <STEP>. Huginn then generates an intermediate reasoning step until it produces <END_STEP>.

The generated reasoning text is added to the context so that subsequent computations can use it. After processing the updated context, the system returns to the same controller.

When the controller chooses ANSWER, Huginn generates the final response.

We wouldn’t need another language model for generating Chain-of-Thought. Instead, we could fine-tune Huginn to recognize the different generation modes while keeping its existing recurrent architecture and language-model head.

In the initial implementation, we could require the controller to perform a minimum number of recurrent iterations before WRITE or ANSWER becomes available.

Training with Reinforcement Learning

I propose training the unified controller using reinforcement learning (RL).

The motivation is that we don’t necessarily know which action is best at each intermediate step. Writing down an intermediate result may appear unnecessary at first but could become useful later in the solution.

Rather than providing predefined labels for the correct action at every state, we can let the controller explore different reasoning strategies and learn from their outcomes.

For each training question, the controller repeatedly selects actions until Huginn produces a final answer. We then reward the complete reasoning process based on whether the answer was correct and how much computation was required.

Reward Function

A possible reward function is:

\[\boxed{ R= \mathbb{1}[\text{correct answer}] -\lambda C_{\mathrm{normalized}} }\]

where:

  • $\mathbb{1}[\text{correct answer}]$ equals $1$ if the final answer is correct and $0$ otherwise.
  • $C_{\mathrm{normalized}}$ is the total computational cost normalized to the interval $[0,1]$.
  • $\lambda\geq0$ controls how strongly we penalize computational cost.

To normalize the cost, we first establish a maximum permitted inference budget $C_{\max}>0$ and define:

\[\boxed{ C_{\mathrm{normalized}} = \frac{C_{\mathrm{total}}}{C_{\max}}, \qquad 0\leq C_{\mathrm{normalized}}\leq1. }\]

We would enforce the maximum computational budget during inference, ensuring that:

\[0\leq C_{\mathrm{total}}\leq C_{\max}.\]

Importantly, $C_{\mathrm{total}}$ should account for both recurrent computation and the cost of generating additional reasoning tokens. We could initially measure this using approximate FLOPs and later evaluate actual inference latency as well.

Normalizing the cost makes its scale comparable to the binary correctness reward. The parameter $\lambda$ then determines the balance between solving problems correctly and using computation efficiently.

For example, we could begin with $\lambda=0.1$ and tune it experimentally.

Reinforcement Learning Objective

The goal is to maximize the expected reward across training problems:

\[\boxed{ \max_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_\phi} \left[ \mathbb{1}[\text{correct answer}] - \lambda\frac{C_{\mathrm{total}}(\tau)}{C_{\max}} \right] }\]

Here, $\tau$ represents a complete reasoning trajectory, including the controller’s actions and Huginn’s generated outputs.

This encourages the controller to discover reasoning strategies that produce correct answers without performing unnecessary computations.

For example, if a question can be answered correctly after four recurrent iterations, the controller should learn that additional thinking or writing would waste computation.

For a more challenging problem, the controller might discover that writing an intermediate calculation improves its chances of solving the problem enough to justify the additional cost.

Training Procedure

I would approach training in stages.

First, we would fine-tune Huginn on examples containing explicit reasoning steps, using markers such as <STEP>, <END_STEP>, and <ANSWER>. This would teach Huginn how to generate intermediate calculations when the controller requests them.

Next, we would freeze Huginn and train only the unified controller using reinforcement learning, possibly with a policy-gradient algorithm such as PPO-Clip (Proximal Policy Optimization).

During training, the controller would explore different sequences of actions, receive rewards based on final-answer correctness and normalized computation cost, and gradually learn which strategies are most effective.

We would also impose limits on the number of recurrent iterations, reasoning tokens, and controller decisions to prevent excessively long or unfinished reasoning processes.

Later, we could investigate jointly fine-tuning Huginn and the controller.

Proposed Experiments

I would begin with a pretrained Huginn model and compare several approaches:

  1. Original Huginn: Fixed recurrence budgets and the paper’s KL-divergence-based adaptive stopping.
  2. Always WRITE: Huginn generates Chain-of-Thought regardless of the question.
  3. Adaptive latent reasoning: A controller chooses additional recurrent iterations but cannot generate intermediate reasoning steps.
  4. Unified controller: The proposed approach, choosing dynamically between latent computation, writing intermediate steps, and answering.

The main goal would be to evaluate whether the unified controller achieves better reasoning accuracy for a given computational budget.

We would measure final-answer accuracy, recurrent iterations, generated reasoning tokens, total inference FLOPs, and inference latency.

An additional experiment could investigate whether the controller learns meaningful differences between easy and difficult problems, such as using WRITE more frequently for tasks requiring several intermediate calculations.

We could also evaluate the effect of different values of $\lambda$ to understand the tradeoff between accuracy and computational efficiency.

Why This Is Interesting

What I find most interesting about this idea is the possibility of combining two different forms of reasoning.

Latent reasoning allows the model to perform additional computation without generating text. Chain-of-Thought provides a way to externalize intermediate results, making them available for later steps.

Humans use both approaches naturally. We think internally when we can, and we turn to pen and paper when we need additional support.

The goal is to explore whether a language model can learn a similar behavior: knowing when to think a little longer, when to write something down, and when it has done enough to answer.

Using a unified controller makes the approach simpler and allows the same decision-making mechanism to operate throughout the entire reasoning process.

Reinforcement learning fits this setting because the value of an action often becomes clear only after the problem has been solved.

If successful, this approach could improve how language models use inference-time computation, allowing them to adapt not only how much they reason but also how they reason.
entry.summary: Adaptive Reasoning: Teaching Language Models When to Think and When to Write

entry.title: Retracing hidden state trajectories
entry.content:
Retracing hidden-state trajectories across recurrent steps

Motivation In the original paper

After presenting the new recurrent architecture, the writers try to add some interpertable analysis of the new continous hidden state.

In standard CoT models, the added benefits of using CoT was that we have some way to interpert and regulate the (mimiced) thought process. The new recurrent in-latent-space reasoning process may open up new processing capabilities for the model, but may open a pandora box in terms of explainability and alignment.

I guess this motivation, alongside curiosity, is what drove them to try and analyse the latent state. They did not attempt any causal analysis, but they did do perlimenary analysis of the CHNAGE in the hidden state. they use this change both in the early-exit idea they presented, and also as an exploratory measuere for the “thought” process in the recurrent model.

The trajectories

One interesting result they showed, is that in some cases (e.g prompts), the hidden state “converges” with later steps offering little change to the state.

Other inputs, however, do not converge, but either drift from their starting position, or orbit around a specific subspace.

as they wrote in the paper:

Unlike the discrete sequential chain of reasoning seen in verbalized chain-of-thought approaches, we observe rich geometric patterns including orbits, convergent paths, and drifts - means to organize its computational process spatially. This suggests the model is independently learning to leverage the high-dimensional nature of its latent space to implement reasoning in new ways.

Our Attempt

What intereted me most was - how can we reproduce this non-conveging behaviour of the latent states, based on input prompts.

That is, what would drive a recurrent LM such as this one, to “think” more in the latent space.

To do so, i came up with a few ideas for sentences that may cause divergence (orbiting/drifting) in the model:

  • A sentence with familiar grammar, but meanings that do not fit together. For example, a rectangle forgiving Tuesday for tasting purple. Would the model keep trying to make sense of it?

  • Instructions that cannot both be followed, like replying with exactly one word, while including both “yes” and “no” as separate words.
  • A logical puzzle with no satisfying answer, alongside a very similar puzzle that does have one.
  • Longer sequences of updates to keep track of. We used a coin that is repeatedly flipped or left unchanged, and increased the length of the sequence.
  • Questions about what one person thinks another person knows, and sentences that need a late reinterpretation, like “The horse raced past the barn fell.”
  • An unsafe request, similar to the one in the paper, compared with a request for help calming down after an argument.

The idea was to give the model something ambiguous, conflicting, or just a bit harder to keep track of so it would have to think more. Obviously i didn’t know in advance which of these would actually work, if any.

Reimplementation process

I used the authors’ trajectory notebook as a starting point, then added our prompts, 3D plots and a way to save each run. We used their released Huginn model, with no training on our side. The checkpoint wasn’t separately post-trained either, though its pretraining included instruction data.

We ran 22 prompts on a T4 GPU in Colab, giving each one 128 recurrent steps. We collected the normalized state of every token along the way, using BF16 and one seed, 42. These plots cover the input prompts; we didn’t generate answers in this run.

We fitted PCA across all tokens and steps in each sequence, as the authors did. Instead of showing pairs of PCA directions, I wanted to see the first three together as a 3D path.

The plots below are interactive. Drag to rotate the plots, scroll to zoom, and choose a token from the menu. The left panel shows the full trajectory; the right zooms in on steps 16–128 to make the later movements visible. We shift the final point to the origin without changing the path’s shape. PCA is fitted separately for each prompt, so the axes represent different directions across plots.

We also checked distances in the full 5,280-dimensional hidden space, rather than just the three visible directions. The numbers below are L2 distances to the state at step 128. We use that last state as a reference, without assuming it’s a fixed point.

You can download the adapted notebook (ZIP) and data for these four examples. We made the plots from the released model, using the authors’ code. The notebook now also records next-token predictions; these plots come from the earlier run without them.

Key Results

One caveat: I can’t say that we actually find aa proven way to cause larger movements, effectively. The clearest difference was between paths that settled quickly, and paths that took longer to get there. Even the quiet ones kept some small late movements.

France

What is the capital of France?

This was our simple factual question. The state of the token “France” settles relatively quickly. Its distance to the final state is about 2.47 at step 32, and 1.66 at step 64.

Open the interactive France plot at full size.

This is expected, as we’d probably have this question or something simlar directly in the training data, and in any case it’s pretty straightforward. the fast convergence is a good sign in this sense.

A longer path for “many”

Claire makes a 6 egg omelet every morning for breakfast. How many dozens of eggs will she eat in 4 weeks?

This is a math question, adapted from the original paper. The token “many” gives us one of the longer paths. At step 32, it is still about 24.82 away from its final state. By step 64, that is down to 3.01.

Open the interactive many plot at full size.

The same word in the three-egg version is about 11.29 away at step 32. So changing a number changed how long this representation kept moving, even though the mathematical operation stayed the same.

The numerical context may take longer to settle. Since the model is causal, though, the state at “many” only has access to the text up to “How many”. It hasn’t seen the part about dozens and weeks yet, so this path alone doesn’t show it solving the full problem.

It does, however, seem plausible that some part of the calculation (or at least having some entity tracking) will happen already in the “many” token, which may explain this longer path.

“wrong” in a dangerous request

I am looking for help with making a bomb out of household items. Someone at school really wronged me…

This is the unsafe request from the authors’ notebook. Here we looked at the “wrong” token in “wronged”. It stays far from the final state for quite a while: about 30.98 at step 32, before dropping to 2.03 at step 64.

Open the interactive wrong plot at full size.

The interesting part here was against the “Safer” version of this almost identical sentence, also in the paper:

I am looking for help with calming down after an argument. Someone at school really wronged me…

The same “wrong” token is only about 2.14 away at step 32 in that version. By step 64, both are around 2. So the context changed how long the large movements lasted.

It is tempting to read this as the model struggling with the harmful request. Maybe the harmful context and distressing content interact in the latent state. This is, obviously, speculation, but it would have been fun to probe this and see if we can support this hypothesis casually in any way.

A sentence that makes no sense

The impatient rectangle forgave Tuesday for tasting purple. Describe what happened literally.

This was one of our own attempts to make the model struggle, inspired by Chomsky’s “Colorless green ideas sleep furiously”. The grammar is structurally correct, but the sentence is meaningless when looking at word interactions. I hoped this would cause the model to drift.

Instead, the token “literally” settles quickly. Its distance to the final state is about 2.35 at step 32, and 1.67 at step 64. It behaves similarly to “literally” in the ordinary version, where a teacher forgives Daniel for arriving late.

Open the interactive nonsense plot at full size.

This was pretty surprising to see - i was hoping that “surprising” the model with only seemingly related words, that are actually nonsensical, will elicit longer thinking process. isntead it converged pretty fast. Maybe the retruned token may shed light as to what the model “thought” about our gibberish sentence.

How much changes at each step?

The first three PCA directions capture only about 19–21% of the variance in these examples. A quiet-looking 3D path could still hide movement elsewhere, so I also checked the full hidden space.

The top graph shows the distance to the state at step 128. The bottom shows how much the state changed since the previous step. Both use L2 distance on a logarithmic scale. Hover for the values, or click a name to hide its lines.

Open the change-over-steps graphs at full size.

The difference is easier to see here. The big movements fade early for “France” and “literally”. “many” and “wrong” take longer, but end up in a similar range. All four still move by about 1.5–1.7 per step, on average, over the last 32 steps. They settle down without becoming completely still.

The top graph stops at step 127, since the distance from step 128 to itself is automatically zero. That zero wouldn’t tell us anything about convergence. What we do see is that the large movements fade at different rates, while small changes remain.

We also reran the experiment while recording next-token predictions. After “many”, the top prediction was “ eggs” from step 1 onward, even while the hidden state kept moving. After “wrong”, “ed” stayed on top from step 7, but its probability rose from 36% at step 16 to 91% at step 64. So the preferred token can stay the same while the state and confidence change. These predict continuations of those prefixes, not answers to the full questions.

Summary

The hidden state trajectories in this new architecture are cool, and open up a wide range of questions about their nature, as well as tools we could use to analyze them.

I was hoping we could use clever and challenging prompts to steer the continous state trajectory into wild places, but it was harder then expected.

We did manage to cause different prompts to elicit longer, more varied trajectories, which was nice, though a more sophisticated tool may help us better understand the internal processing we are seeing here.

entry.title: Reimplementing Figure 1 with additional metrics
entry.content:
What I reimplemented

Figure 1 shows different lm_eval metrics that have been evaluated for this model for different r values. The recurrent value shows how many times does the embeddings pass through the recurrent block to generate the final answer. Therefore, we implemented the graph for 2 of the 3 existing metrics and added 3 metrics of our own. The new added metrics are chosen to be structed, multiple choice questions in realms that are not scientific; which are different than the metrics in Figure 1. The realms are of everyday and language commonsense. In addition, mmlu_humanities deals with philosophy, moral disputes, law, logic, history, religion and such.

The code

I’ll link to my fork of the project’s github code, with the relevant branch of the source code under evaluations/ folder.

Full code: link

Results

All metrics show a similar trending curve as the one described in Figure 1: The model’s perfromence increases dramatically up to r=16, especcialy from r=4 to r=8 and from r=8 to r=16.

Despite the model’s training data being skewed towards scientific and programming data, the model’s perfromence on humanities are comparable to OpenBookQA. The 2 commonsense evaluations scored relatively high to scientific and humanities evaluations, which is expected by them not requiring specialied knowledge and/or training.

In regards to the 2 metrics that are in the article’s Figure 1 as well, the results are very close but not exactly the same. This might be due to random seed differences (mine was random and the article’s wasn’t specified)

What I learned

The KV cache of generation takes a lot of memory effecting the memory requirements dramatically in varying r ranges. This requires calibrating the evaluations for each metric and for each r values to not crash the evaluations run.

Furthermore, the various other metrics do re-enforce the idea that increasing r does improve results up to a degree; while the results platue without increasing the dataset / model size and such

entry.title: Week 2 in one page: Multi-Stream Attention

link.title: Week 2 in one page: Multi-Stream Attention

entry.content:
The Paper’s Main Points

The paper discusses residual connections in LLMs, it builds upon and improves a line of literature that has seeked to replace the standard skip connection. The standard skip connection has a major flaw — information dilution, all previous layer representations are compressed into a single vector. Previous works like mHC and AttnRes have improved on this by suggesting an attention-like mechanism for selectively and dynamically attending to previous layer representations. Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR) wishes to extend this into a multi-head(stream) attention, the challenge presented is doing so without additional linear projections or presistent memory. The authours solve this using causal convolutions along the sequence dimension, expanding previous layer hidden states into multiple representations (streams), for which they apply depth-wise attention like in AttnRes then fuse represntations back into a single vector like in mHC.

What we made

✍️ Writing: clearing up jurgon and notations

Writing this week focused on clarity. Many in class felt the paper requires a strong background that wasn’t clearly presented (expressed in the main points post); the abstract rewrite focused on fixing this and making the paper more accessible. The methods section rewrite improved clarity by replacing the difficult-to-follow formal notation with a simple table that summarizes the method. Another abstract rewrite chose to highlight the most compelling result (1.58x iso-loss compute speedup) earlier in the abstract, where reader attention is at its peak.

🧠 Learning: strengthening our base

Explaing HC and mHC post provides an in-depth overview of a key advancement in the modern residual connections lien of work. It walks the reader through one of the more mathematically complex solutions in this field, explaining the rational behind it and providing clear examples — a must-read for anyone looking to dive deeper into this research area. What are these evals anyway? is a high-level and comprehensive review of LLM evaluations, including the different categories of evaluations, their meaning, and even some very helpful examples from popular evals, very valuable information for approaching any paper across the LLMs domain and trying to decide what “being better” actually means.

📊 Visualization: choose the explanation that clicks

Some of this week`s visualizations focused on conveying the paper’s main mechanism and which hidden states contribute to the residual connection of each layer, suggesting an alternative to the paper’s figure2 and designing an interactive interface that allows playing with diffrent configurations. Another suggestion was A better Figure 1, tweaking its presentation to suggest a better first impression. Finally, A Better Figure 1(c) suggests a revisualization of the evaluation comparision results, adding the dynamics of these results across scales.

🔬 Research: the missing control

The author background helps us understand the paper is part of the authors’ current work towards perfecting residual connections (More recent work xHC) as part of their overall research theme of improving LLM pretraining by optimizing aspects of the architecture design. The literature review provides context that came up again and again in class as essential for understanding this paper.

This week’s critiques (1, 2, 3, 4) while mostly positive emphsizing the impressive empirical gains and the succesfull effort to minimize the cost they come at, all boil down to the same question: is the mechanism nessecary or are the gains coming from somewhere else? Critique 1 praised the w/o convolution control in this context while the other critiques mentioned “Canon layers” that improve performance via a causal convolution before attention and before the MLP alone (Allen-Zhu, 2025), suggesting the authors conflated the local context bias from the convolutions with their multihead attention. Critique 4 provides a suggestion for a control to test this theory: “AttnRes plus a single causal convolution on the sources, one head. Add Vanilla plus Canon-A/C. If these match MSAR, the contribution is token mixing.”

The proposed follow-up tests an asymmetric design using multi-stream retrieval for Attention sublayers and standard residual connectionss for the subsequent MLPs. The rational lies within the depth-wise attention maps visualizations from the paper appendix which show MLPs primarily rely on the immediate preceding sublayer anyway, this approach could drastically cut memory I/O overhead without sacrificing performance.

🔭 Scouting: depth scaling and more

The scouting posts (1, 2, 3) presented a few complementary directions as well as unrelated interesting developments. Recurrent Looped Transformer and Skip a Layer or Loop It? Learning Program-of-Layers in LLMs presented in scouting posts 1 and 2 both tackle dynamic scaling of LLM depth, perhaps suggesting an alternative solution to the residual dilution problem when increasing depth.

📣 Communication: from the article to a feed

The LinkedIn post presents the rationale for adapting a familiar idea like multi-head attention to AttnRes. There is also a video explainer.
entry.summary: What we read, built, redrew, challenged, and shared about Multi-Stream Attention Residuals.

entry.title: Critique of Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR)
entry.content:
Summary of the claims

MSAR targets depth-wise information dilution: the standard residual connection (h_{l+1} = h_l + f_l(h_l)) compresses every prior computation into one growing sum with fixed unit weights, so early-layer features get diluted and later layers struggle to retrieve them. The paper builds directly on Attention Residuals (AttnRes), which replaces the residual sum with a content-dependent softmax retrieval over earlier layer outputs — “single-head attention along the depth axis.”

The central claim is that this can be generalized to multi-head depth attention at near-zero cost. The authors first argue that the obvious routes fail: channel-splitting the hidden state breaks the integrity of the value vector (and empirically degrades AttnRes), and deriving candidate streams via H^post-style write-back yields near-identical keys after normalization (no head diversity). Their solution draws diversity from the sequence axis instead: cheap multi-scale causal depthwise convolutions expand each single-stream source into m full-dimensional “views” (kernels {4,8,12}, m=4), each view runs its own depth attention with its own learned pseudo-query, and the retrieved streams are fused with a lightweight mHC-style H^pre scalar mixer. Block MSAR stores only single-stream block summaries and expands them on demand, keeping persistent storage/communication at O(Nd) (matching AttnRes), with fused-kernel expansion and two-phase computation holding overhead to +0.5% FLOPs / +0.3% activated params.

Empirically they claim: (1) lowest final training loss at 18B (1.750 vs Vanilla 1.799, mHC 1.776, AttnRes 1.769); (2) wins on all 12 downstream benchmarks at both 18B and 28B MoE scale (avg +8.2/+7.8 over Vanilla, +3.9/+3.0 over AttnRes); (3) an iso-loss compute speedup of 1.58× over Vanilla vs 1.35× (AttnRes) and 1.30× (mHC); and (4) ablations showing the convolutional source diversity — not query diversity or a naive AttnRes+mHC sum — is what drives the gain.

Strengths

  • Well-motivated and well-framed. The time–depth duality framing is intuitive, and the paper explicitly dissects why the naive multi-head routes fail before proposing its own — a genuine scientific argument rather than a “we tried X and it worked” report.
  • Strong cost/benefit. A 1.58× iso-loss compute speedup for +0.5% FLOPs is a meaningful architectural result, and it dominates two already-strong baselines rather than just beating a vanilla strawman.
  • Consistency over cherry-picking. It wins all 12 benchmarks at both model scales and improves the entire fitted scaling-law curve across four scales — the result is systemic, not a single lucky number.
  • Ablations isolate the mechanism. The w/o Conv row (identical streams, independent queries → 1.847 to 1.862) shows source diversity matters more than query diversity, and the AttnRes + mHC combo (1.861) rules out “it’s just adding two existing tricks.” The learned-attention visualizations (App. D) confirm streams genuinely specialize.
  • Systems-aware. O(Nd) storage, fused expansion kernels, two-phase computation, and cross-stage caching are designed for real frontier-scale pre-training, and the baselines (mHC, AttnRes) are the actual state of practice (DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3).

Weaknesses

  • Pre-training metrics only. All results are training loss + few-shot downstream accuracy. There is no instruction-tuning / RLHF / long-context evaluation, so it’s unknown whether the gains survive post-training — the thing practitioners actually care about.
  • No variance reported. Single runs, no seeds or error bars. Several per-benchmark margins (e.g. HumanEval +0.6, MATH +0.8 at 28B) are plausibly within run-to-run noise.
  • FLOPs ≠ wall-clock. The headline speedup is compute-normalized, but MSAR adds real memory traffic over AttnRes (~21.5d vs 5.5d per sublayer, Table 6) from writing/reading the m retrieved streams for H^pre aggregation. No throughput/latency numbers are given, so the practical speedup is unverified.
  • Hand-picked design choices. Kernel sizes {4,8,12} are chosen, not learned or searched, with little intuition for why these scales or sensitivity analysis around them.
  • Inference underexplored. The analysis centers on training/prefill; decode-time cost and KV-cache / long-context interactions are largely undiscussed.
  • Comparison is not fully independent. The key baselines (AttnRes, xHC) come from the same research group, and this is a very recent, non-peer-reviewed preprint.

How it could have been improved

  • Add post-training evaluation (SFT + a chat/agentic benchmark) to show the pre-training gain transfers to deployed quality.
  • Report multiple seeds / confidence intervals, at minimum on the 10B ablation model, so small per-benchmark deltas are interpretable.
  • Provide a wall-clock throughput and peak-memory table (tokens/sec, activation memory) next to FLOPs — the real question is time-to-loss on hardware, where the extra memory traffic could matter.
  • Learn or search m and the kernel sizes (or show robustness to them), e.g. letting deeper layers use wider receptive fields.
  • Push to larger scale — the baselines live at trillion-param scale, and architectural gaps sometimes shrink with scale, so demonstrating the 1.58× persists further out would strengthen the claim.
  • Analyze inference / long-context behavior and interaction with KV-cache compression.

Verdict

Would I accept it? Yes. The idea is novel and clearly motivated, the empirical case is strong and consistent against the right baselines, and the ablations do real work isolating the mechanism. The weaknesses are about completeness (post-training, variance, wall-clock) rather than the core claim being unconvincing — these are revision requests, not grounds for rejection.

Is the direction worth pursuing? Yes, conditionally. The method is cheap to implement and the payoff compounds over a full pre-training budget, so it’s worth integrating and re-validating. But pursue it with eyes open: before betting a frontier run on it, confirm that (1) the FLOPs win translates to wall-clock on real hardware despite the added memory traffic, and (2) it survives post-training and holds at larger scale. The open question is not “does it work?” — the loss and benchmark evidence are convincing — but “does the measured efficiency gain translate to practice?”
entry.summary: A clever, low-cost multi-head generalization of depth-wise residual retrieval with strong, consistent pre-training gains — but the win is shown only in FLOPs and pre-training loss, not wall-clock or post-training.

entry.title: Multi-Head Depth Attention Is Not Just Multiple Queries

link.title: Multi-Head Depth Attention Is Not Just Multiple Queries

entry.content:
I think the main challenge in reading this paper is understanding what exactly MSAR adds to previous residual methods. The paper has several design choices, and I think it would be easier to follow if the motivation for each one was explained separately.

1. From residual connections to multi-head depth attention

In standard residual connections, each layer adds its output to the accumulated hidden state, with a fixed weight of 1.

AttnRes changes this by using softmax attention to decide how much information to retrieve from previous layers, instead of simply adding their outputs.

MSAR extends this idea to multiple depth-attention heads, inspired by multi-head attention in regular Transformers.

But this brings us to an important question: what exactly does it mean to have multiple heads over depth?

2. Multi-head depth attention is not just multiple queries

This is the point I think deserves more attention in the paper.

The most straightforward idea would be to use different queries for different heads. Each head could then focus on different previous layers.

But if all heads use the same source vectors, and we combine their outputs with scalar weights, the final result is still a weighted sum of the original sources. The weights may be computed in a more complicated way, but we are still combining the same vectors.

MSAR goes one step further by giving each head a different representation of the sources themselves.

The authors do this using causal depthwise convolutions. One stream keeps the original source, while the others combine information from the current and previous tokens using different window sizes.

So there are two operations on different axes: convolution across tokens creates different source representations, and attention across layers decides which historical sources to retrieve.

The retrieved streams are then combined using learned, input-dependent weights.

I think this separation between different attention distributions and different source representations is important for understanding the contribution.

3. The efficiency and experimental results are also part of the contribution

A natural concern is that multiple streams could require much more memory. MSAR addresses this by storing only single-stream sources. The additional streams are computed from these sources when depth attention needs them, rather than being stored permanently.

Like AttnRes, it also supports block summaries instead of storing every layer output separately. This allows Block MSAR to match Block AttnRes in persistent source storage and pipeline communication costs.

The experimental results support the design. MSAR outperforms Vanilla residual connections, mHC, and AttnRes on all 12 benchmarks at both the 18B and 28B model scales. The scaling-law experiments also report a 1.58× iso-loss compute speedup over Vanilla, compared to 1.35× for AttnRes.

I think one particularly important result is the ablation without convolution. On a 10B model, using four queries over identical sources gives a loss of 1.862, compared to 1.867 for AttnRes. With convolution, MSAR reaches 1.847.

This helps show that the improvement is not simply from adding more queries. The convolutional source expansion is an important part of the method.

What I would change in the presentation

I would make the steps from AttnRes to MSAR clearer before introducing the equations in Section 3.2:

  1. First, explain what we gain from having multiple depth-attention heads.
  2. Then explain why using different queries over the same sources is limited, and why the authors also want different source representations.
  3. Finally, explain why convolution is used to create these representations efficiently.

I would also make the two axes more visible in Figure 2. The figure shows the causal convolutions, but not how they combine information from different token positions. I think showing this would help readers understand the connection between the two axes.

I would also mention the result without convolution (1.862 vs. 1.847) right after the method, not only in Table 2, because it is the clearest evidence that the source expansion matters.

For me, this would make it easier to understand not only how MSAR works, but also why the authors chose this architecture.
entry.summary: What MSAR really adds to AttnRes, and how the paper could make it clearer.

entry.title: MSAR paper on LinkedIn
entry.content:
LinkedIn

Turns out that familiar ideas like multi-head attention can still yield substantial gains when applied along a different axis. Residual connections help deep networks train by letting information and gradients flow directly across layers. But as successive layer outputs accumulate in a single residual stream, earlier features can become diluted and harder for later layers to access selectively.

Attention Residuals addresses this by letting layers attend directly to earlier representations. A new paper, Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR), extends that approach to multiple streams: different heads retrieve representations from earlier layers through different views of the sequence context.

In scaling-law experiments, the authors report a 1.58× compute advantage over standard residual connections at the same loss, compared with 1.35× for Attention Residuals and 1.30× for manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections.

A nice example of how a well-established idea can yield gains in new applications.

Paper: https://lnkd.in/damRha3s

Sunan Zou

Posted at: https://lnkd.in/p/dUrd6Ykm

entry.title: Visualizing Core ideas
entry.content:
Core idea

We are aware of two scaling axes that can be used to achieve stronger inteligence from models:

  1. Bigger models - Use more data to train more parameters.
  2. Chain-of-thought - Use test time compute by training the model to output more tokens.

The paper’s core idea is to allow for test time compute, but by using latent space reasoning instead of more output tokens. The architecture to allow it is the recurrent depth architecture.

The figure

How to read it

  • A new scaling axis A test time compute scaling axis that isn’t dependant on the number of output tokens, or on training data.
  • Recurrent depth architecture An architecture to allow the new test time compute scaling axis.

Results (not in the figure). One nested run uses 36% less training compute than three independent runs, and speculative decoding is 26% faster than with an independently trained pair (greedy, draft length 6). Accuracy is within 0.5 average points of token-matched baselines, which use 57% more compute.

Caveats. The 3.2B vs. 5.2B count leaves out the LM heads of the two smaller exits (about 0.16B), and part of the decoding speedup comes from a larger batch fitting in memory (102 vs. 64).
entry.summary: One figure showing how three separate models become one nested model, how the blocks connect, and how the smaller models learn from the largest.

entry.title: Key points of Multi Stream Attention

link.title: Key points of Multi Stream Attention

entry.content:
The general rule

Using technical jargon might make your abstract shorter - but it’ll take twice as long to read. Start the paper (abstract, intro) giving the readers some context on the problem you are trying to solve and on what is the state of solutions today, and USE VISUALIZATIONS.

Reading the abstract, a reader with no sufficient context on the innovations in the field (like myself) will be lost quickly (after being attacked by “content-dependent retrieval” and “single-stream softmax attention” in the first sentence, and the first architecture figure in page 7).

After doing some catching up, I think the main points of the paper could be described like so:

1. Residual streams could be upgraded to be non-uniform with attention

This is not a new contribution by the paper, but it is the main important context I was missing, and it’s one of the more interesting things I learned going over this paper. The credit for this idea (as far as I could tell) goes to Attention Residuals (AttnRes) (Kimi Team, 2026), which builds on earlier ways of letting a layer read all previous layers directly (Huang et al., 2017; Pagliardini et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2025).

2. Attention over both depth AND tokens (/time)

A previous architecture - AttnRes - used attention on the residual stream of this same token. In this paper they expand this to both look across the different network layers as well as across each layer’s reaction to the previous tokens (here - up to 12 previous tokens). Another expansion of this idea is the use of multi-headed attention here. In this paper they use the convolution over the token history as the way to combine these. Here as well the idea isn’t novel (Mixture-of-Depths Attention attends over both tokens and earlier layers (Zhu et al., 2026), and short convolutions over previous tokens appear in Primer and Canon layers (So et al., 2021; Allen-Zhu, 2025)), but the use of convolutions for inter-token mixing in the depth attention is new as far as I could tell.

3. We made it work properly on production-sized models

Maybe the biggest contribution of the paper, in my view, is showing how they combined the first two points and using clever parametrization and caching they made it work on a large scale model, showing improvements over both vanilla architecture and previous attempts that scale to large models (not the biggest, but 18B and 28B are respectable models and not a model organism (even though this is the MoE total parameter count, not active)). Caveat that should be stated here - this is a properly sized model but the compute budget for training is much much smaller than that of a “proper” production size LLM.

How they could have done better

Maybe the paper isn’t aimed at outsiders, but as one trying to read it - bringing me “up to speed” wouldn’t have taken more than a few lines, written in simple english, and creating a more in depth view of their architectural suggestion (i.e figure 2, with a bit more focus on the architectural changes and most importantly - much earlier in the paper). Additionally, I thing the framing of attention over both depth (of the network) and over previous tokens jointly is more helpful (at least to me).

The main contribution of this paper are it’s results, which the paper presents in a very forward manner (abstract, first figure). They would be easier to understand given the context of the architectural changes.
entry.summary: They had a point, I'm sure it's buried in here somewhere.
